parole.significato: Usually added to foreign words to form nouns of professions, sciences, etc.; also to form names of countries or lands.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -ia or Ancient Greek -ία (-ía), -εία (-eía); found only in words borrowed from other languages (compare German, French -ie).

parole.significato: Usually added to foreign adjectives to form abstract nouns, like English -ity (sometimes with more concrete meanings: e…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -itatem, the accusative of -itas; found only in words borrowed from other languages (compare English -ity, German -ität, French -ité, Italian -ità, Spanish -idad, Portuguese -idade, Romanian -itate).

parole.significato: Usually added to foreign nouns or adjectives to form verbs with the sense "to make (something) be (what is denoted by t…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -izāre, itself from Ancient Greek -ίζειν (-ízein); found only in words borrowed from other languages (compare English -ize, -ise, French -iser, Spanish, Portuguese -izar, Italian -izzare), German -isieren, Russian -изировать (-izirovatʹ)).

parole.significato: Usually added to foreign verbs to form nouns of actions or processes, like English -ation, -tion.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -atio; found only in words borrowed from other languages (compare English -ation, French -ation, Spanish -ación, German -azion, Italian -zione).

parole.significato: Usually added to foreign words to form adjectives.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin -ivus; found only in words borrowed from other languages (compare English -ive, French -if, German -iv).

parole.significato: abbot (the (male) leader of a Catholic abbey or monastery)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin abbās (“father”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”).

parole.significato: ablative case (one of the inflections in some languages denoting the starting point of an action)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ablātīvus.

parole.significato: abortion (premature termination of pregnancy before the full 22 weeks, spontaneous or artificial)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin abortus.

parole.significato: abstract (that does not exist in real space and even in principle cannot be perceived by any instruments)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin abstractus.

parole.significato: adjective (a word used to qualify or modify a noun)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin adiectīvus (“adjective”).

parole.significato: administrator, manager (male official who performs certain tasks pertaining to the organization and functioning of an i…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin administrātor, a nominalized form of the verb administrō (“to attend upon, to assist”), i.e. “he who assists, attends upon.”

parole.significato: adverb (a word used to modify a verb, an adjective, an adverb, a phrase or a clause)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin adverbium.

parole.significato: lawyer
parole.testo: From Latin advocātus.

parole.significato: aphorism
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós, “pithy phrase containing a general truth”), from ἀφορίζω (aphorízō, “I define, mark off or determine”), from ἀπό (apó, “off”) + ὁρίζω (horízō, “I divide, bound”), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).

parole.significato: academy (the highest scientific and research institution in a country)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Latin acadēmīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove of trees and gymnasium outside of Athens where Plato taught; from the name of the supposed former owner of that estate, the Attic hero Akademos.

parole.significato: accent, stress (pronunciation emphasis on a specific syllable)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin accentus, (ad + cantus), from the verb accinō (“to sing to”), from ad (“to”) and canō (“to sing”).

parole.significato: acroterium (sculptural decoration at the corners or apex of building gables)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin acrōtērium.

parole.significato: act, action
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin ācta (“register of events”), the plural form of āctum (“decree, law”), from agō (“put in motion”).

parole.significato: active voice(s) (the liveliest, most energetic members of an organization or team)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin activus indirectly through some other European language.

parole.significato: accusative case (the grammatical case that marks the direct object)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin accūsātīvus.

parole.significato: aqueduct (a bridge-like structure used to carry water over a river or depression; an artificial canal used to carry wat…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin aquaeductus (“conveyance of water”), itself a compound of aqua (“water”) and dūcō (“to lead”, “to bring”).

parole.significato: algebra (the branch of mathematics that studies generic numbers regardless of their actual numeric value)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Medieval Latin algebra, from Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr, “reunion, resetting of broken parts”) in the title of al-Khwarizmi's influential work الْكِتَاب الْمُخْتَصَر فِي حِسَاب اَلْجَبْر وَالْمُقَابَلَة (al-kitāb al-muḵtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala,

parole.significato: amulet
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin amulētum.

parole.significato: analytic, analytical
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Latin analyticus, from Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικός (analutikós). With -isks ending.

parole.significato: analysis
parole.testo: Ultimately from Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis), from ἀναλύω (analúō, “I unravel, investigate”), from ἀνά (aná, “on, up”) + λύω (lúō, “I loosen”).

parole.significato: anatomy (science that studies the form and structure of living organisms)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin anatomia, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνατομία (anatomía), a word attested only once, in a quotation in a Latin text by Caelius Aurelianus, from ἀνατέμνω (anatémnō, “to cut up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) and τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: antimony (metalloid chemical element, quite toxic, with atomic number 51.)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin antimonium, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: anal (of or relating to the anus)
parole.testo: From Latin ānus (“anus”) + -āls. Clearly not derived as such in Latvian, but borrowed and adapted from another European language.

parole.significato: device, appliance, set, machine, contraption
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Latin apparātus, the perfect passive participle of apparō (“to prepare”).

parole.significato: applique (decorative design made by applying materials to a surface)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin applicātiō, from applicō (“apply”), made into a 4th-declension feminine noun ( + -ācija). The sense "applique" is probably due to the influence of the French term appliqué.

parole.significato: apostrophe (the ’ character, used in some languages as a punctuation mark and as a diacritical mark in others)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin apostrophus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (apóstrophos, “accent of elision”), a nominal use of an adjective derived from the verb ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “to turn away”).

parole.significato: the month of April (the fourth month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin Aprīlis (“of the month of the goddess Venus”), perhaps based on Etruscan 𐌀𐌐𐌓𐌖 (apru), from Ancient Greek Ἀφροδίτη (Aphrodítē, “Venus”).

parole.significato: architecture
parole.testo: From Latin architectūra.

parole.significato: archivist
parole.testo: From Latin archīvārius.

parole.significato: archive
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin archīvum.

parole.significato: arch (bow-shaped arrangement between two supports)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately a borrowing from Latin arcus (“bow”), in feminine form (compare French arche (“bow”) and Late Latin arca, also ultimately from arcus).

parole.significato: arsenic (metalloid chemical element, quite poisonous, with atomic number 33)
parole.testo: From Latin arsenicum, from Ancient Greek ἀρσενικόν (arsenikón, “yellow arsenic”) (influenced by ἀρρηνικός (arrhēnikós, “potent, virile”)), ultimately (via Semitic) from Middle Iranian *zarnīk (“gold-coloured”), compare Persian زرنیخ (zarnix, “orpiment”), زرنی (zarni).

parole.significato: article
parole.testo: From Latin articulus.

parole.significato: artery (blood vessel taking oxygenated blood from the heart to the rest of the body)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin artēria, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría, “windpipe, artery”).

parole.significato: association
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin associātiō.

parole.significato: aster (several decorative plants of the family Asteraceae, genus Aster or Callistephus, with variously colored flowers)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin aster, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr).

parole.significato: astronomy (science that studies celestial bodies, their structure, development, and interrelations)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Latin astronomia, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονομία (astronomía), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) and νόμος (nómos, “arranging, regulating”), adapted to Latvian patterns (-ija).

parole.significato: atmosphere
parole.testo: Ultimately from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”)

parole.significato: atom (smallest part of a chemical element that still has its chemical properties)
parole.testo: From Latin atomus (“smallest particle”) (borrowed via some other European language), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: the month of August (the eighth month of the year)
parole.testo: From Late Latin Agustus, from Latin augustus (“month of August”), from the agnomen Augustus (“venerable”) of Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus. Distantly related to the adjective augsts.

parole.significato: author
parole.testo: Ultimately from New Latin autor, from Latin auctor. Compare Lithuanian autorius, Polish autor, German Autor.

parole.significato: beryllium (chemical element, atomic number 4)
parole.testo: From New Latin beryllium, from beryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”), + -ium.

parole.significato: Belgian (i.e., a man born in Belgium)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Belgae (“Belgians”), the name of a group of Gallo-Germanic tribes living in the area of present-day Belgium, apparently from Proto-Celtic *bolg-, *belg- (“to swell (with anger, battle fury)”), i.e., originally this tribal name would have meant “the people who swell with anger or

parole.significato: a Briton, a British man, a man born in Great Britain; a citizen of the United Kingdom
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin Brittō or its Celtic equivalent (see Brython), probably via some other European language (cf. German Brite, Russian бритт (britt)).

parole.significato: a Bulgarian man, a man born in Bulgaria
parole.testo: Probably via other European languages, ultimately from Medieval Latin Bulgarus, from Old Church Slavonic блъгаринъ (blŭgarinŭ), itself from the self-designation of Turkic Bulgars, from Proto-Turkic *bulgar (“disturber, disturbing”), active noun/adjective of *bulga- (“to create a state of disorder; t

parole.significato: center (a notable or important point in a mathematical or physical body)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin centrum (“central”) (itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point”)).

parole.significato: central, central station (main, leading part, usually of some device or system)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from New Latin centrāle, the neuter form of the adjective centrālis

parole.significato: cent (a currency subunit (one hundredth of the main unit) used with several currencies, among which the dollar and the…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin centum (“hundred”).

parole.significato: caesium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 55.)
parole.testo: From Latin caesius (“sky-blue”), in reference to the radiation spectra.

parole.significato: date (point in time)
parole.testo: Probably derived from Latin datum (“given”, past participle).

parole.significato: dative case
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin datīvus.

parole.significato: moron, mentally retarded (having impaired mental development)
parole.testo: Ultimately borrowed from Latin dēbilis (“weak; lame”), via some other European language.

parole.significato: the month of December (the twelfth and last month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin december (“tenth month”), from Latin decem (“ten”); December was the tenth month in the Roman calendar.

parole.significato: dolphin (maritime mammals of the family Delphinidae)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately a borrowing from Latin delphīnus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís), from δελφύς (delphús, “womb”).

parole.significato: dynamics
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from Latin dynamica.

parole.significato: director ((male) administrator or manager in an institution or enterprise)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin dīrēctor, from the Latin past particle form dīrēctus of the verb dīrigō (“to set straight, to direct”).

parole.significato: discipline (well-defined and established order or system of rules which is obligatory to some group of people; obedienc…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin disciplina (“instruction”) (cf. also discipulus “student”), from discō (“to learn”).

parole.significato: dissertation
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin dissertātiō. Featuring -ācija ending.

parole.significato: discussion, debate (conversation or debate, typically in public, where opposed opinions are presented and contrasted)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin discussiō, made into a fourth declension feminine noun.

parole.significato: dragon, winged serpent (reptilian monster that spits fire and devours people and animals)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin dracō, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “a serpent of huge size, a python, a dragon”), probably from δέρκομαι (dérkomai, “to see clearly”).

parole.significato: safety (situation, conditions in which one is not under threat, not in danger, not being disturbed)
parole.testo: From drošs (“brave, safe, sure”) + -ība. Possibly a calque of Latin sēcūritās. Compare Lithuanian saugumas, which may also be a calque from Latin.

parole.significato: a Dane, a man born in Denmark
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Dania (“Denmark”)

parole.significato: demon, devil (supernatural evil being)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin daemon (“genius, guardian spirit”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “dispenser, god, protective spirit”).

parole.significato: effect (result, consequence, action or state generated by some cause; vivid impression)
parole.testo: A borrowing, ultimately from Latin effectus (“an effect, tendency, purpose”) (from efficiō (“to accomplish, to complete”)), probably via some other European language.

parole.significato: ejaculation (forcible ejection of semen from the urethra, usually accompanied by orgasm)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin ēiaculātiō (“shooting or gushing forth”), made into a 4th declension feminine noun ( + -ija).

parole.significato: to ejaculate
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin ēiaculor (“to hurl, to shoot out”) (cf. perfect passive participle ēiaculātus), from ē (“out”) + iaculor (“throw, dart”), from iaculum (“a missile, a dart”), from iaciō (“to throw, to hurl”).

parole.significato: ecliptic (Earth's orbital plane)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ecliptica.

parole.significato: economy, savings (frugal, effective use of resources, leading to the saving of time or resources; the savings achieved…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) and νόμος (nómos, “law”).

parole.significato: economy (system of management of capital and resources, their production, distribution, and consumption)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) and νόμος (nómos, “law”).

parole.significato: existence, living, life, subsistence, survival (the fact of existing, of being or staying alive)
parole.testo: Via some other European language (cf. French existence, German Existenz), ultimately borrowed from Latin existentia (“existence”).

parole.significato: to exist, to be
parole.testo: Via some other European language (cf. French exister, German existieren), ultimately borrowed from Latin exsistō (“to exist”).

parole.significato: expert (a person with extensive knowledge or ability in a given subject)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin expertus.

parole.significato: electric, electrical
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from New Latin ēlectricus (“electrical; of amber”) from ēlectrum (“amber”) + -icus (“adjectival suffix”), from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”). With -isks ending.

parole.significato: emblem
parole.testo: From Latin emblēma, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma).

parole.significato: encyclopedia (a scholarly publication that provides news on one or more industries and where the material is arranged a…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin encyclopaedīa.

parole.significato: erotica (eroticism, sensuality; literature, art, situations that arouse erotic, sexual feelings)
parole.testo: Ultimately from the neuter plural form of Latin eroticus (“amatory”), from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós), probably borrowed via some other European language (maybe German erotisch).

parole.significato: erosion (destructive effect of natural external forces (wind, water, etc. on the surface of the earth, its soil, rocks,…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin ērōsiō, an action nominal derived from the verb ērōdō (“to gnaw away, to corrode”). It was adapted to fit Latvian grammatical patterns ( + -ija).

parole.significato: etymology (science that studies the origins of words and morphemes).
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”) (from λόγος (lógos)).

parole.significato: ethnic (relating to a group of people having common racial, national, religious or cultural origins)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin ethnicus (“pagan, heathen”), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company”, later “a people or nation, heathens”).

parole.significato: evolution (change, progress, development transformation)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiō (“the act of unrolling, unfolding or opening (of a book)”), from ēvolūtus, perfect passive participle of ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, and volvō (“roll”).

parole.significato: fact (a true, real event or phenomenon)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin factum (“a deed, act, exploit; in Medieval Latin also state, condition, circumstance”), neuter of factus (“done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (“to do, to make”).

parole.significato: the month of February (the second month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin Februārius, of the month of purification, from februa, the Roman festival of purification, plural of februum.

parole.significato: federation, confederation, league (an association that includes other associations, organizations)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Latin foederātiō (“federation”).

parole.significato: phenomenon (an unusual occurrence or entity)
parole.testo: From Latin phaenomenon (“appearance”), from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).

parole.significato: philosophy (the study of ultimate, fundamental principles in nature, thought, and spirit)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía), from φίλος (phílos, “beloved, friend”) and σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”) (with the suffix -ία (-ía), Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: physiology (branch of biology that studies the processes of life, the functioning of living organisms and their parts)
parole.testo: Via some European language, ultimately from Latin physiologia, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογία (phusiología, “natural philosophy”), from φύσις (phúsis, “nature”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, treatise”) with the suffix -ία (-ía) (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: fluorine (chemical element, with atomic number 9; under normal conditions, a poisonous gas)
parole.testo: From Latin fluor (“flow”).

parole.significato: phosphorus (nonmentallic chemical element with atomic number 15)
parole.testo: From Latin phosphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “the bearer of light”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, to carry”).

parole.significato: frequency, rate (number of repetitions of a periodic phenomenon)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin frequentia (“frequency”), probably via German (compare Frequenz, with qu = [kv]).

parole.significato: hairstyle, hairdo
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, borrowed from German Frisur, from French frisure, with ending Latinized based on Latin -ūra.

parole.significato: galaxy (independent, coherent gravitationally maintained system composed of stars, planets and other celestial bodies)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin galaxias (“galaxy; Milky way”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “Milky Way”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”). The form with -ka suggests that the borrowing went through the adjectival form γαλακτικός (galaktikós), rathe

parole.significato: gallium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 31)
parole.testo: From Latin Gallia (“Gaul”), named by its discoverer Lecoq. It was claimed that Lecoq had named the element after himself, since gallus is the Latin translation of the French le coq, but Lecoq denied this in an article of 1877.

parole.significato: germanium (metalloid chemical element with industrial uses, with atomic number 32)
parole.testo: From Latin Germania (“Germania, land of the Germanic peoples”).

parole.significato: rodent
parole.testo: From grauzt (“to gnaw”) + -ējs (agent suffix). Calque of Latin rōdēns (“gnawer”).

parole.significato: governor
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin gubernator, from Ancient Greek κυβερνήτης (kubernḗtēs, “steersman, pilot, guide”), from κυβερνάω (kubernáō, “to steer, to drive, to guide, to act as a pilot”).

parole.significato: hafnium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 72.)
parole.testo: From Hafnia, the Latin name of the city of Copenhagen.

parole.significato: hassium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 108.)
parole.testo: From Hassia, the New Latin form of the name the German state of Hessen, the location of the institute where the element was first synthesized.

parole.significato: synonym of nīlzirgs
parole.testo: From Latin and New Latin hippopotamus (via some other European language), from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + ποταμός (potamós, “river”).

parole.significato: holmium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 67.)
parole.testo: From Holmia, the Latin name of the city of Stockholm, the hometown of Per Teodor Cleve, one of the discoverers of this metal.

parole.significato: homonym (one of two or more words that coincide partially or completely in pronunciation and/or spelling but differ sig…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin homōnymum, from Ancient Greek ὁμώνυμον (homṓnumon), neuter singular form of ὁμώνυμος (homṓnumos, “having similar names”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) and ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

parole.significato: chromium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 24)
parole.testo: From New Latin, from French chrome, from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”).

parole.significato: humor (good-natured, playful attitude; the capacity to recognize and understand what is funny or comical)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin umor (“moisture”), from the ancient theory that the moods and dispositions of the human psyche were related to bodily fluids.

parole.significato: humane, compassionate (showing compassion, kindheartedness, respect in relations with others; such that it expresses su…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin humanus (“human, humane”).

parole.significato: helium (chemical element, noble gas)
parole.testo: From New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”) (because its presence was first theorised in the sun's atmosphere).

parole.significato: idea (a concept or mental image that reflects reality in a person's consciousness)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”).

parole.significato: identity
parole.testo: From Latin identitās, with -itāte suffix.

parole.significato: imbecile (having serious problems in mental development)
parole.testo: Ultimately borrowed from Latin imbēcillus (“weak, feeble”) (literally “without a staff”), probably via some other European language.

parole.significato: emperor (male monarch of an empire; his title)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin imperātor (“emperor, commander, general”).

parole.significato: empress consort (the wife of an emperor)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin imperātrīx (“female ruler”).

parole.significato: empire (a monarchic state, especially a large one)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin imperium (“power, command”), made into a 4th declension feminine noun ( + -ija).

parole.significato: indium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 49.)
parole.testo: From Latin indicum (“indigo”), from Ancient Greek Ἰνδικὸν (Indikòn, “Indian dye”).

parole.significato: industry
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin industria (“diligence, activity, industry”). Features -ija ending.

parole.significato: insect (arthropod with a three-part body, three pairs of legs, sometimes also wings (Order: insecta); less specifically…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin insectum (“with a divided body; cut up”), the perfect passive participle of insecō (“to cut up”), from in- and secō (“to cut”), based on the idea that an insect's body is "cut into" three sections. The Latin term is a calque of Ancient Gre

parole.significato: inspirer (a man who inspires, who incites)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin inspirator.

parole.significato: inspiration (a sudden surge in mental activity that increases one's creative productivity; a sudden desire to create)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Late Latin inspīrātiō, from inspīrō (“to breathe into”), made into a 4th declension feminine noun ( + -ācija).

parole.significato: inspire, incite (to stimulate the creative powers of someone, to cause the desire to create, to work, to act)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Latin īnspīrō (“to breathe in”).

parole.significato: institute
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin īnstitūtum.

parole.significato: instrumental case
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin instrumentālis.

parole.significato: interesting (that which causes interest)
parole.testo: A borrowing, ultimately from the present participle of Latin interesse (“to concern; to make a difference”), probably via other European language (e.g., German interessant, or French intéressant).

parole.significato: interjection (a word or phrase used as an exclamation, often as an expression of emotion)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin interiectiō (“interjection”).

parole.significato: interpretation (the detailed explanation of a thought, idea, text)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Latin interpretatio (“interpretation”).

parole.significato: punctuation (the set of punctuation marks in a given language; the use of punctuation marks in a given language)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin interpunctiō, from inter (“between”) and punctiō (“pricking, puncturing”), from the verb pungo (“to prick, to puncture, to sting”).

parole.significato: intonation (the melodic curve of an utterance that expresses part of its content)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin intonātio (a Medieval Latin formation), made into a 4th-declension feminine noun ( + -ācija).

parole.significato: to intonate, to produce an intonation (to pronounce a syllable, a word, a sentence etc. with a specific tonal melody)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin intonō (“to thunder, to resound”), made into a second-conjugation verb (ending -ēt).

parole.significato: intuition
parole.testo: Derived via other European languages from Medieval Latin intuitio (“a looking at, immediate cognition”), from Latin intueri (“to look at, consider”), from in (“in, on”) + tueri (“to look, watch, guard, see, observe”). Compare Lithuanian intuicija, Russian интуи́ция (intuícija), Belarusian інтуі́цыя

parole.significato: intimate (realting to a person's inner world or personal life; deeply personal)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from Latin intimus (“innermost”), the superlative form of intus (“within”), from in.

parole.significato: irrational (not understandable by the mind, not rational, not reasonable)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin irratiōnālis, from ir- + ratiōnālis. The sense "radical; involving mathematical roots" is perhaps related to the fact that the square roots of most integers are irrational.

parole.significato: unreal (such that it isn't, cannot be real, in reality; imagined, made up, existing only in fantasy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin irreālis (“unreal”), adapted to fit Latvian patterns (suffix -āls).

parole.significato: Italic; a member of the ancient Italic peoples of primitive Italy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin italus, itself possibly a borrowing from Oscan 𐌅𐌝𐌕𐌄𐌋𐌉𐌞 (víteliú), a name for the southwestern tip of the boot of Italy (today's Calabria), possibly a cognate of Latin vitulus (“calf”), meaning perhaps “land of cattle.” Other theories include the name of an ancient or legendary le

parole.significato: the month of January (the first month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin Iānuārius (“(month) of Janus”).

parole.significato: the month of July (the seventh month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin iūlius (Gaius Julius Caesar's month), perhaps a contraction of Iovilios (“descended from Jove”).

parole.significato: the month of June (the sixth month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin iūnius, the month of the goddess Iuno (“Juno”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *yuwn̥kós, from *h₂óyu (“vital force, youthful vigor”).

parole.significato: calcium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 20)
parole.testo: From New Latin calcium, derived by Sir Humphry Davy in 1808, from Latin calx (“lime, limestone”), because it occurs in limestone.

parole.significato: calendar (listing of days, weeks, and months that compose a year; the corresponding printed material, as a book, table,…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin calendarium (“account book”), from calendae (“the first day of the month”), from calō (“to announce solemnly, to call out (the sighting of the new moon)”).

parole.significato: campaign
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”), from Latin campus (“field”).

parole.significato: fireplace
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin camīnus.

parole.significato: cathedral (a church governed by a bishop)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cathedrālis.

parole.significato: monastery, cloister, convent (the building and adjacent land inhabited by an order of monks)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin claustrum (“portion of monastery closed off to laity”), from Latin claustrum (“enclosure”), a nominal use of the neuter past participle of claudo (“to close”).

parole.significato: colon (the punctuation mark : which usually indicates a longer pause)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin cōlon (“a member of a verse of poem”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κῶλον (kôlon, “a member, limb, clause, part of a verse”).

parole.significato: comma (punctuation mark (,) usually indicating a short pause; sign used to separate the integer from the decimal part o…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin comma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κόμμα (kómma), from κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”). The term was made into a 1st-declension masculine noun with an additional final t, probably following the Ancient Greek declensional paradigm (κόμμα

parole.significato: comfortable, convenient (where one feels at ease; having all comforts)
parole.testo: A borrowing, via other European languages (cf., e.g., French, English comfortable, German komfortabel, all with reflexes of the Latin suffix -abilis), ultimately from Late Latin confortō (“strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (“strong”).

parole.significato: comedy, comicality, buffoonery (that which causes disapproval because of its ridiculousness)
parole.testo: Probably the same as komisks: via Latin comicus, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós).

parole.significato: comical (expressing facts, ideas, etc. in a humorous, mocking way; typical of comedy)
parole.testo: Via other European languages (cf German komisch, French comique), ultimately borrowed from Latin comicus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós), adapted to fit Latvian patterns ( + -isks).

parole.significato: humorist, comedian (stage performer who plays a comical role, especially in circus or theater)
parole.testo: Probably the same as komisks: via Latin comicus, ultimately borrowed from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós).

parole.significato: comedy (an artistic work (play, movie, book, etc.) in which conflicts and characters are portrayed in a way that causes…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin cōmoedia (itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía)), adapted to fit Latvian patterns ( + -ija).

parole.significato: comet (celestial body composed mostly of ice, dust and gas, having a “tail” of matter caused by the solar wind)
parole.testo: From Latin cometa, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs, “long-haired”), referring to the tail of a comet, from κόμη (kómē, “hair”).

parole.significato: conception (image, idea, or notion formed in the mind)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin conceptiō. Featuring -ija ending.

parole.significato: confederation (union of sovereign nations, usually based on a treaty or written agreement)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Latin confoederātiō (“confederation”).

parole.significato: denomination, creed
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Latin cōnfessiō, cōnfessiōnem (“confession, acknowledgment, creed or avowal of one's faith”). With -ija ending.

parole.significato: conjunction (a word used to join words or phrases into sentences)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin coniūnctiō (“conjunction”).

parole.significato: concrete (appearing in the complete diversity of all its features, properties, connections and relations)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin concrētus (“migled; hardened, solidified”), past participle of concernō (“to mix, swift, mingle”).

parole.significato: contest, competition
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin concursus. Sense 1 derives from Russian ко́нкурс (kónkurs), while sense 2 most likely derives from German Konkurs, itself from Latin concursus creditorum (“assembly of creditors”). Compare Lithuanian konkursas (“competition”).

parole.significato: constitution (basic law)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cōnstitūtiō. Featuring -ija suffix.

parole.significato: continent (large landmass, completely or almost completely surrounded by seas and oceans)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Latin continēns (accusative form continēntem), the present participle of the verb continēo (“to contain”) used as a noun.

parole.significato: cosmology (science that studies the universe as a whole)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cosmologia, from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world, universe”) and λόγος (lógos, “speech, oration, study”) + -ija.

parole.significato: criterion, criteria (essential characteristics that distinguish entities or phenomena; a test for comparing, distinguis…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from New Latin criterion, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion, “a test, a means of judging”), from κριτής (kritḗs, “a judge”), from κρίνω (krínō, “I judge”).

parole.significato: crocodile
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin crocodilus, via some other European language.

parole.significato: quality
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin qualitas (“quality”). Featuring -itāte suffix.

parole.significato: laboratory assistant, laboratory technician
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin labōrāns, present participle of labōrō. Compare German Laborant, Polish laborant, Russian лабора́нт (laboránt).

parole.significato: laboratory
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Medieval Latin laboratorium, made into a 4th declension feminine noun ( + -ija). Compare Russian лаборато́рия (laboratórija).

parole.significato: a Latin man; a male member of the people of Latium (today's Lazio) in ancient Italy
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin latīnus (“Latin”), itself derived from Latium, the name of the region in Central Italy where the ancient Latins lived (and where Rome is located).

parole.significato: leopard (large spotted wild cat, Panthera pardus)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin leopardus, from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos), from λέων (léōn, “lion”) and πάρδος (párdos, “panther”).

parole.significato: synonym of burtstabiņš
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin littera.

parole.significato: lithium (chemical element, atomic number 3)
parole.testo: From New Latin lithium, from lithia (in reference to Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”)) + -ium, a name created in 1818 by Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius (in Latvian: Jenss Jākobs Bercēliuss) to stress this metal's mineral origin, unlike other previously known alkalis of vegetable origin.

parole.significato: logarithm (power to which a certain base must be raised in order to obtain a given number)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from New Latin logarithmus, a term coined by Scot mathematician John Napier from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word, reason”) and ἀριθμός (arithmós, “number”).

parole.significato: locative case
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin locātīvus.

parole.significato: chandelier (illumination device that hangs from the ceiling and consists of several candle or light bulb holders)
parole.testo: Via other European languages (cf. e.g. French lustre), ultimately borrowed from Latin lustrō (“to purify; to make bright”).

parole.significato: lutetium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 71.)
parole.testo: From Lutetia (“the Latin name of Paris, the capital of France”).

parole.significato: a male given name from Latin, equivalent to English Lucius
parole.testo: From Latin Lūcius, a common Roman praenomen deriving from lux (“light”).

parole.significato: magnesium (chemical element, a light, silvery metal, with atomic number 12)
parole.testo: From New Latin magnēsium, from Magnēsia (“region in Thessaly”).

parole.significato: the month of May (the fifth month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin māius (“Maia's month”), from Maia, a Roman earth goddess, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *magya (“she who is great”), from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (“great”).

parole.significato: manganese (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 25)
parole.testo: From Latin Magnesia, from Ancient Greek Μαγνησία (Magnēsía).

parole.significato: manuscript (a handwritten text, usually an old one)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin manuscriptum (“writing by hand”), from Latin manus (“hand”) and scrīptus, the past participle of scrībō (“to write”), apparently a calque of Germanic origin (cf. earlier Middle High German hantschrift, hantgeschrift, Old English h

parole.significato: the month of March (the third month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin mārtius (“month of the god Mars”), from earlier Mavors.

parole.significato: mathematics (science that studies the nature and relations of number and form)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin mathēmatica (“mathematics”), from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, study, learning”).

parole.significato: material
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin māteria (“material, substance”)

parole.significato: matrix
parole.testo: From Latin matrix, matricis.

parole.significato: medicine (the science of human diseases, their causes, course, diagnosis, treatment and prevention; set of techniques t…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin medicīna (“the healing art, medicine, a physician's shop, a remedy, medicine”), feminine of medicinus (“of or belonging to physic or surgery, or to a physician or surgeon”), from medicus (“a physician, surgeon”), from medeor (“to heal”).

parole.significato: mechanics (branch of physics that studies the motion of bodies and their resulting interaction)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin mechanicus (“of or belonging to machines or mechanics, inventive”), from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious, inventive”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”).

parole.significato: mechanism, engine (system of elements in a machine, device, etc. that allows it to function by means of the motion of i…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin mechanismus, from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós, “pertaining to machines or contrivance, mechanic, ingenious, inventive”), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, contrivance”).

parole.significato: mass
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin missa.

parole.significato: metaphysics (branch of philosophy that studies the first principles meant to explain all that exists; the specific meta…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from Latin metaphysica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká), from the title of the collection by Aristotle μετὰ τὰ φυσικά (metà tà phusiká), a collection that comes after (= μετά (metá)) Aristotle's collection entitled τὰ φυσικά (tà phusiká), from φυσικός

parole.significato: method (way, process to achieve a goal or complete a task; system of principles and techniques that governs and regulat…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos, “pursuit of knowledge, investigation, mode of prosecuting such inquiry, system”), from μετά (metá, “after”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way, motion, journey”).

parole.significato: microscope (instrument for observing small objects)
parole.testo: Internationalism, from New Latin microscopium (or via some other European language), from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “to look at”).

parole.significato: mineral (naturally occurring inorganic material with characteristic chemical and physical properties)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin minera (“ore”).

parole.significato: minister (government official who runs a government ministry)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin minister (“an attendant, servant, assistant, a priest's assistant or other subordinate official”), from minor.

parole.significato: minute (unit of time, 1/60 of an hour)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin minūta (“diminished (hour)”).

parole.significato: mobile (which can move, which can be moved relatively easily)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin mōbilis (“easy to be moved, moveable”), from moveō (“move”).

parole.significato: modern (pertaining to the society, science, technique, art of a certain time period, usually the current one)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from Late Latin modernus, from Latin modo (“just now”), originally ablative of modus (“measure”); hence, by measure, “just now.”

parole.significato: molecule (smallest part of an element or compound that still preserves its chemical properties)
parole.testo: From New Latin mōlēcula.

parole.significato: molybdenum (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 42.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin molybdaenum, from Ancient Greek μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead”), because the two elements are so similar they were often confused.

parole.significato: coin (a piece of currency, usually metallic and circular)
parole.testo: Via other European languages (cf. Russian моне́та (monéta)), ultimately borrowed from Latin monēta (“mint; money, coinage”), from Monēta, one of the surnames of the goddess Juno, in whose temple money was coined.

parole.significato: morality (historically determined system of norms, rules, and principles that regulate human action in society and in r…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin mōrālis.

parole.significato: national (relating to a nation or people)
parole.testo: From nācija (“nation”) + -āls. Clearly not formed in Latvian, but borrowed as such from some other European language (ultimately from New Latin nationalis).

parole.significato: petroleum, oil (naturally occurring liquid petroleum)
parole.testo: From Latin naphtha, from Ancient Greek νάφθα (náphtha).

parole.significato: neutral (showing neutrality; not being aligned, not taking sides in a conflict)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin neutrālis, changed and adapted to Latvian patterns (eu > ei).

parole.significato: nominative case
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Latin nōminātīvus.

parole.significato: norm (rule, principle, which regulates people's relations in a society)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin norma (“a carpenter's square; rule, standard”).

parole.significato: the month of November (the eleventh month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin november (“ninth month”), from Latin novem (“nine”); November was the ninth month in the Roman calendar.

parole.significato: numeral (a word used to indicate a number)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin numerālis (“numeral”).

parole.significato: nation (historically evolved stable community of people, sharing a common language and cultural traits, a common territ…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin natio (“nation, race, birth”).

parole.significato: sodium (chemical element, an alkali metal, with atomic number 11)
parole.testo: From New Latin natrium.

parole.significato: ocean (one of the largest natural masses of water, situated between continents)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin Ōceanus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós, “Oceanus”), a water deity.

parole.significato: the month of October (the tenth month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin Octōber (“eighth month”), from Latin octō (“eight”). October was the eighth month in the Roman calendar.

parole.significato: ontology (branch of philosophy that studies being in its most general terms, its principles and structure; the ultimate…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin ontologia, from Ancient Greek ὤν (ṓn, “on”), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “being, existing, essence”), and λόγος (lógos, “study of”), with the suffix -ia (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: operation (a set of surgical procedures for treatment or diagnosis)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin operātiō.

parole.significato: opposition
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin oppositiō, translating ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from the past participle stem of classical Latin oppōnō (“to set against”).

parole.significato: orbit (path of one object, especially celestial bodies, around another)
parole.testo: From Latin orbita (“track, path, impression, mark”), from Latin orbis (“ring, circle, world”), itself of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: to organize
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately derived from Medieval Latin organizō.

parole.significato: ornithology (science that studies birds)
parole.testo: Ultimately from modern Latin ornithologia, coined by Ulisse Aldrovandi from Ancient Greek ὀρνιθολόγος (ornithológos), from ὄρνις (órnis) and λόγος (lógos) with the suffix -ία (-ía) (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: orthography, correct spelling (the officially correct way to spell words in a given language)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin orthographia, itself a borrowing from Hellenistic Ancient Greek ὀρθογραφία (orthographía), from ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) and γράφω (gráphō, “write”).

parole.significato: oasis
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”).

parole.significato: patient
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin patiens.

parole.significato: palm tree
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin palma.

parole.significato: panther (large cats of genera Panthera and Puma, especially leopards and cougars)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin panthēra, from Ancient Greek πάνθηρ (pánthēr, “panther”).

parole.significato: paradox (a contradiction between statements assumed to be simultaneously true; a contradiction to something known or be…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin paradoxum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).

parole.significato: participle (a verb form having both verbal and adjectival or adverbial properties)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin participium (“participle”).

parole.significato: grammatical particle (a word that does not belong to any word classes but has a clear grammatical function)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin particula (“small part, particle”), the diminutive form of pars (“part, piece”).

parole.significato: liabilities (debts, taxes, interest and other money that a company has to pay; part of a budget that lists them)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin passivus, probably via some other European language, adapted to fit Latvian patterns ( + -īvs).

parole.significato: penis
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.

parole.significato: parchment (material made from animal skin and used for writing)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin pergamīna, from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós, “of Pergamon”), which is named for the Ancient city of Pergamon (modern Bergama) in Asia Minor, where it was invented as an expensive alternative for papyrus.

parole.significato: person
parole.testo: From Latin persōna (“person”).

parole.significato: plum tree
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin pruna, from Latin prunum.

parole.significato: political (relating to politics)
parole.testo: From politika (“politics”) + -isks. Probably borrowed as such, ultimately from Latin politicus, Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), with the ending changed under the influence of words with the suffix -isks.

parole.significato: polonium (nonmetallic, sometimes considered metalloid, chemical element, with atomic number 84.)
parole.testo: From New Latin Polonia (“Poland”), Marie Curie's home country.

parole.significato: position
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin positio (“a putting, position”), from ponere (“to put, place”, verb), past participle positus (“put, placed”)

parole.significato: preposition (a word used to build a phrase with a noun to express an adverbial notion)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin praepositiō (“preposition”).

parole.significato: president
parole.testo: Internationalism, ultimately from Latin praesidens.

parole.significato: object, thing
parole.testo: From priekš- + mest, calque of Latin obiectum. Compare Russian предме́т (predmét) and Polish przedmiot.

parole.significato: prism
parole.testo: Via some other language, from Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρῖσμα (prîsma).

parole.significato: process
parole.testo: From Latin prōcessus (“progression, progress, process”), perfect passive participle of prōcēdō (“to advance, proceed”), from prō- + cēdō (“to go, move, proceed”).

parole.significato: product (object or substance made as a result of human labor or of some labor-like activity)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin prōductus, perfect participle of prōdūcō (“to bring forward”).

parole.significato: professor (a man who has the highest teaching position in a college or university; such a position)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin professor (“declarer, person who claims knowledge”), from the past participle stem of profiteor (“profess”).

parole.significato: progression (a sequence of numbers in which every term differs from its predecessor by a well-defined rule)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin prōgressiō (“progression, advancement, growth”), made into a feminine 4th-declension noun ( + -ija).

parole.significato: progress (development, esp. to a higher, fuller, more advanced state; transition from a lower to a higher level)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin prōgressus (“an advance”), from the participle stem of prōgredī (“to go forward, advance, develop”), from pro- (“forth, before”) + gradi (“to walk, go”).

parole.significato: project (a scheme for the building of something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prōiectum (“projection”) (via some other European language), a perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth, extend; expel”).

parole.significato: pronoun (a word used to refer anaphorically to a noun or noun phrase)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin prōnōmen (“pronoun”).

parole.significato: to prostitute (to make someone work as a prostitute, i.e., having sex for profit)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin prōstituō (“to prostitute”), made into a 2nd-conjugation verb (ending -ēt).

parole.significato: prostitute (a woman who sells sex)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin prōstituta, the feminine form of prōstitutus, past participle of prōstituō, from pro- (“for, before”) + statuō (“to set up, to erect”).

parole.significato: to provoke
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin prōvocāre.

parole.significato: psalm (sacred song)
parole.testo: From Latin psalmus, derived from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós).

parole.significato: psychology (the science of human behavior and the human mind)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Late Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, study”), with the suffix -ia (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: powder
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pulvis, pulveris.

parole.significato: rational (sensible, reasonable)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ratiōnālis, probably via another European language.

parole.significato: referendum (direct popular vote or a proposed law or amendment)
parole.testo: From Latin referendum (“what ought to be brought back, reported”), the gerundive form of referō (“to bring back, report”).

parole.significato: loudspeaker (electromechanical device that converts an electric signal into audible sound)
parole.testo: Via other European languages (cf. Czech reproduktor “loudspeaker”), ultimately derived from Latin re- “again” + producō “to produce”, in nominalized form (suffix -tor), i.e. “one which reproduces.”

parole.significato: republic (country where power and sovereignty rests with representatives elected by the people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rēs publica (“republic”) via other European languages, from rēs (“thing”) and publica (“public[fem.]”), literally “the public thing.”

parole.significato: reputation
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin reputātiō.

parole.significato: to restore (bring back to a previous condition or state)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately derived from Latin rēstaurāre.

parole.significato: result (the outcome, the consequence, the effect of some action, event, situation)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin resultō (“to spring forward, to rebound”), the frequentative form of the past participle of resiliō, from re- (“back”) and saliō (“to jump, to leap”).

parole.significato: real (that which indeed exists, which is not invented or imagined)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin reālis (“actual”) (from rēs (“matter, thing”), of unknown origin), adapted to fit Latvian patterns (cf. suffix -āls).

parole.significato: registrar, record keeper; hospital or polyclinic receptionist (official in charge of registration, or of keeping record…
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Medieval Latin registro (see reģistrs), apparently with the agent suffix -(a)tor.

parole.significato: register (list, usually official, containing, e.g., names of people, property, events)
parole.testo: Via some other European language) (probably German; compare Register), from Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerō (“to record, carry back”), from re- + gerō (“to carry, bear”).

parole.significato: rite (a religious custom or ceremony; the specific details of this custom or ceremony)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin rītus.

parole.significato: ritual
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin rītuālis, from noun rītuum (“rite”), + adjective suffix -ālis.

parole.significato: pink (having the whitish red color of, e.g., roses)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin rosa, perhaps via German rosa.

parole.significato: rubidium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 37.)
parole.testo: A New Latin word derived by German chemist Robert Bunsen in 1861, from Latin rubidus (“red”), because its spectrum has two red lines.

parole.significato: ruby (red, semi-transparent type of corundum, valued as a precious stone)
parole.testo: Via other European languages (cf. Russian руби́н (rubín)), ultimately borrowed from Latin rubeus (“red, reddish”).

parole.significato: rhenium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 75.)
parole.testo: From Rhenus, the Latin name of the river Rhine.

parole.significato: lettuce (herbaceous plant of the family Asteraceae, esp. Lactuca sativa, cultivated for its edible leaves)
parole.testo: Via other European languages (cf. French salade, German Salat, Russian сала́т (salát)), ultimately a borrowing from Vulgar Latin salāta, from saliō (“to salt”), from sal (“salt”), apparently initially a reference to the sauce (e.g., “salted vegetables”).

parole.significato: sanction (an approval, by an authority, generally one that makes something valid)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin sanctiō, from sanctus.

parole.significato: sex, gender (the two groups in which most living beings can be divided, according to their role in the reproductive pro…
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin sexus (“sex, gender”).

parole.significato: sexual (relating to sex, to one's sex life)
parole.testo: Ultimately from sekss (“sex”) + -āls. Probably not formed in Latvian, but borrowed as such from some other European language (e.g., Latin sexualis).

parole.significato: second (SI unit of time, 1/60 of a minute)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin secunda, short for secunda pars minuta (“second diminished part (of the hour)”).

parole.significato: selenium (nonmetallic, sometimes considered metalloid, chemical element, with atomic number 34.)
parole.testo: A New Latin word derived by Swedish chemist Berzelius in 1818, from Ancient Greek σελήνη (selḗnē, “moon”).

parole.significato: the month of September (the ninth month of the year)
parole.testo: From Latin september (“seventh month”), from Latin septem (“seven”); September was the seventh month in the Roman calendar.

parole.significato: silicon (metalloid chemical element with atomic number 14)
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin silex (“silica”).

parole.significato: synonym (one of two or more linguistic elements with identical or at least similar meanings)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”), from σύν (sún, “with”) and ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

parole.significato: synthesis
parole.testo: From Latin synthesis, from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις (súnthesis, “a putting together; composition”), from συντίθημι (suntíthēmi, “put together, combine”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “set, place”).

parole.significato: system (collection of organized elements; way of organizing or planning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).

parole.significato: situation (a set of circumstances, usually one that directly influences or determines something)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin situātiō (“position, situation”), from situō (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”).

parole.significato: scandium (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 21)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin scandium, from Latin Scandia (“Scandinavia”).

parole.significato: scandal (loud dispute, quarrel, brawl)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin scandalum (“that on which one trips, cause of offense”, literally “stumbling block”), from Ancient Greek σκάνδαλον (skándalon, “a trap laid for an enemy, a cause of moral stumbling”).

parole.significato: social (relating to society)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin sociālis (“of or belonging to a companion or companionship or association, social”), from socius (“a companion, fellow, partner, associate, ally”), from sequor (“follow”). The form was adapted to Latvian patterns (ending -āls).

parole.significato: sperm, semen (generative substance of male animals)
parole.testo: From Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”).

parole.significato: spore
parole.testo: From Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed, a sowing”).

parole.significato: status quo (the state of things)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin status quō.

parole.significato: status (set of features provided by law to characterize some juridical or physical person, or a country, territory or o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin status.

parole.significato: scholarship (study allowance)
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Latin stipendium (“pay, stipend”).

parole.significato: studio, school (training provider, typically in the performing arts, where new performers learn performing skills)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin studium (“study”). The meaning of "artistic workshop" was apparently first attested in Italian (see studiolo).

parole.significato: to study at a university or college
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Latin studeō (“to dedicate oneself, to study”).

parole.significato: noun (a word used to refer to an entity, concept or idea)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin substantīvus (“substantive, self-existent”).

parole.significato: table (data arranged in rows and columns)
parole.testo: From Latin tabula

parole.significato: talent (special physical or mental skill for a certain area of activity, especially when inborn)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin talentum (“weight, monetary unit”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “weight, monetary unit”). The “gift” meaning is probably a metaphor, based on the "money" meaning (“rich” → “gifted”).

parole.significato: tantalum (metallic chemical element, with atomic number 73.)
parole.testo: A New Latin word derived by Swedish chemist Anders Gustaf Ekeberg in 1802, from Latin tantalus.

parole.significato: text
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin textus (“style or texture of a work”), perfect passive participle of texō (“to weave”).

parole.significato: tellurium (metalloid chemical element, with atomic number 52.)
parole.testo: From Latin telluris (“earth, ground”), genitive of tellus, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: temperature
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin temperātūra.

parole.significato: theology (branch of scholarship that studies and interprets a body of teaching belonging to a certain religion)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin theologia, from Ancient Greek θέος (théos, “god”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, study”), with the suffix -ia (Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: type (a model having some defining characteristics; an object with certain characteristic features, properties)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately borrowed from Latin typus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”).

parole.significato: toxic, poisonous (having harmful effects on the organism)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin toxicus (“poisoned”), from Latin toxicum (“poison”), from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón) φάρμακον (phármakon, “poison for use on arrows”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”).

parole.significato: topography (science that develops methods for measuring the surface of a region and displaying it on a plan or map)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Latin topographia, from Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía), from τόπος (tópos, “place”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to write”) + -ija.

parole.significato: tradition
parole.testo: From Latin traditio.

parole.significato: transparent (such that one can see through it)
parole.testo: A borrowing, probably via other European languages, ultimately from Medieval Latin trānspārēns, present participle of trānspāreō (“to show through”).

parole.significato: troglodyte, caveman (member of an ancient human species that supposedly lived in caves)
parole.testo: Via other Euroepan languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin trōglodyta (“cave dwelling people”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs, “one who dwells in holes”), from τρώγλη (trṓglē, “hole”) and δύω (dúō, “to get into”).

parole.significato: tiger (large striped wild cat, native to Asia; Panthera tigris)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin tigris, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek τίγρις (tígris), possibly from Iranian.

parole.significato: university, college (important institution of higher education, usually consisting of several faculties)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately a borrowing from Late Latin ūniversitās (“university”), accusative form ūniversitātem, adapted to Latvian patterns ( + -itāte).

parole.significato: utopia
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from New Latin Ūtopia, the name of a fictional island, possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not, no”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”).

parole.significato: vaccine
parole.testo: From Latin vaccīnus.

parole.significato: version, variant, option
parole.testo: Via some other European language (maybe Russian; compare вариант (variant, “version”)), from Latin variāns, the present active participle of variō (“to change”).

parole.significato: verb (a word that indicates an action, event or state; the head of the predicate)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin verbum (“word”).

parole.significato: version (one of several different descriptions or explanations of a fact, event, etc.)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, from Medieval Latin versiō (“a turning”), from Latin vertō (“to turn”).

parole.significato: vocative case
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin vocātīvus.

parole.significato: vowel
parole.testo: A borrowing, via some other European language, ultimately from Latin vōcālis (“voiced”).

parole.significato: vocal (relating to voice, to singing)
parole.testo: A borrowing, via some European language, ultimately from Latin vōcālis (“voiced”).

parole.significato: ethics (the science of morality)
parole.testo: Via some other European language, ultimately from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: genitive case
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin genitīvus.

parole.significato: geology (science that studies the composition, structure, and development of the Earth)
parole.testo: Probably via some other European language, ultimately from New Latin geologia, from Ancient Greek γῆ (gê, “earth”) and λόγος (lógos, “word, study”) + -ija.

parole.significato: (ancient) German; a member of one of the ancient Germanic peoples of primitive Germania
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin Germānus, a term introduced by Julius Caesar from a Gaulish word for a group of tribes living in Northeastern Gaul (probably originally the name of one of these tribes). Of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly Celtic/Gaulish).

parole.significato: Celt, a man belonging to one of the (present and past) Celtic peoples or of Celtic descent
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin Celtæe (“Celts”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Κελτοί (Keltoí).

parole.significato: surgery
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin chirurgia, from Ancient Greek χειρουργία (kheirourgía), from χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). Featuring + -ija suffix.

parole.significato: chemistry (science that studies the composition, properties, structure and changes of substances)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately from Latin alchēmia, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā, “art of alloying metals”) (which contains the suffix -είᾱ (-eíā), Latvian -ija).

parole.significato: China aster (decorative plants, Callistephus chinensis of the family Asteraceae, with variously colored flowers)
parole.testo: Via other European languages, ultimately borrowed from Latin aster, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr).
